o: After processing the first k queries, each index i must be decremented to exactly zero, where each covering query contributes its val at most once (we select a subset of indices per query, so index i can pick any subset of the vals of queries covering it). We need the minimum k making every index achievable. Feasibility is monotone in k (more queries only add options), so binary search on k; for a fixed k, each index independently needs a subset of its available vals summing exactly to nums[i] — a subset-sum test. Tiny constraints (n <= 10, q <= 1000, nums[i] <= 1000, val <= 10) make bitset subset-sum per index essentially free.
k: Monotonicity in k enables binary search on the answer.
Per index, feasibility = subset-sum: can some subset of the vals of the first k queries covering i sum to nums[i]?
A bitset (or big-integer bitmask) shifted by each val solves subset-sum in O(q * 1000 / wordsize).

a.n: Approach 1: Binary search + per-index bitset subset sum
a.i: Binary search the smallest k such that every index passes. For each index, OR-shift a bitmask by each covering val among the first k queries and test whether bit nums[i] is set (nums[i] = 0 always passes).
s: Define feasible(k): for each index i, build bitmask over the vals of queries 0..k-1 covering i; pass iff bit nums[i] reachable.
Return the found k or -1 if even k = q fails.
a.t: O(q log q * n * S/w) where S = 1000 bits — comfortably fast for the given limits
a.sp: O(S) per index for the bitmask

w: Feasibility is monotone because each added query only enlarges every index's reachable-sum set. Pitfall: each query's val can be used at most once per index (subset, not multiset), and nums[i] = 0 is trivially satisfied. Follow-up: with large n you would flip to a per-query sweep with per-index bitmasks updated incrementally.
